title: Matrix Similarity After Cyclic Shifts
statement:
You get an `m x n` integer grid `mat` and an integer `k`; rows are numbered from 0. Perform the following round `k` times:

- every row with an even index rotates one place to the left (its first value moves to the end);
- every row with an odd index rotates one place to the right (its last value moves to the front).

Return `true` when the grid after all `k` rounds is exactly the starting grid, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: All rows of mat have the same length
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating all `k` rounds one rotation at a time works, but a row of length `n` returns to its start after every `n` rotations, so only `k % n` of them matter. Rotating a row left by `shift` places means the value now at column `col` came from column `col + shift` (wrapping around); rotating right means it came from `col - shift`. Build that final row directly and compare it with the original.

## Approach

1. Let `cols` be the row length and `shift = k % cols`.
2. For each `row`, fill `moved`: an even row takes `original[(col + shift) % cols]`, an odd row takes `original[(col - shift + cols) % cols]`.
3. Compare `moved` with `original` cell by cell; any difference means the grid changed, so return `false`.
4. If every row matches, return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`cols = 3`, `k = 4`, so `shift = 1`. Row 0 is `[1, 2, 3]`; rotating left once gives `moved = [2, 3, 1]`. Already at `col = 0`, `moved[0] = 2` differs from `original[0] = 1`, so the answer is `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n): each cell is placed and compared once.
- Space: O(n) for the `moved` row.

## Pitfalls

- Reduce `k` modulo the row length; `k` can be larger than `n`.
- In JavaScript `%` keeps the sign of the left side, so add `cols` before taking `(col - shift) % cols`.
- The direction does not change the answer for a single row (a row equals its left rotation by `s` exactly when it equals its right rotation by `s`), but simulating each direction faithfully avoids having to argue that.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cols` | length of every row |
| `shift` | rotations that matter, `k % cols` |
| `row`, `col` | current row and column |
| `original` | the row as given |
| `moved` | the row after all rotations |

narration.2: Every row has the same length, so read it once from the first row.
narration.3: A row is back where it started after every cols rotations, so only k % cols of them matter.
narration.5: Handle the rows one at a time; each row moves independently of the others.
narration.7: moved will hold this row as it looks after all k rounds.
narration.8: Fill every column of the rotated row.
narration.9: Even rows rotate left, odd rows rotate right.
narration.10: After a left rotation by shift, column col holds the value that was shift places to its right.
narration.12: After a right rotation, column col holds the value that was shift places to its left; adding cols keeps the index non-negative.
narration.15: Now compare the rotated row with the original, column by column.
narration.16: Does any cell differ from where it started?
narration.17: Then the grid changed, so the answer is false.
narration.21: Every row came back unchanged, so the grid is the same as before.
